A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PRMBench, with the same authors, core dataset and error taxonomy. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 15 models, detailed benchmark metrics, step-position analyses and few-shot experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark evaluations and adds model results, a human performance study and Best-of-N experiments in Tables 6, 9 and 10.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction procedure retains PRM800K source solutions, GPT-4o error injection, QwQ-generated alternative solutions and filtering. The supplied generation and critic-evaluation prompts are substantively unchanged. Best-of-N is an additional evaluation, without an established change to the proposed benchmark method.

E1.justification: The 6,216-instance, nine-category PRMBench dataset is retained. v3 adds outcome-selection evaluation on GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench and MMLU: models select among eight candidate responses, expanding task coverage beyond classifying annotated reasoning steps.

E2.justification: Table 3 expands from 15 to 25 models, adding Qwen2.5-Math PRMs, Pure-PRM and open LLM critics including DeepSeek-R1, alongside a human reference. Appendix Table 10 includes further comparators such as WizardMath-7B and MetaMath-70B. The new Best-of-N comparisons include majority voting and pass@8 references. Figure 1 replaces Skywork-7B with ReasonEval-34B.

E3.justification: The new Best-of-8 protocol samples QwQ-Preview-32B responses, multiplies step scores to rank candidates and measures selected-answer accuracy; generative judges use 200 items per benchmark. Human evaluation uses 450 items, 50 per category, divided among three annotators. The existing PRMScore, two-shot setup and 394-item o1-mini evaluation remain.

E4.justification: New Section 5.4 and Appendix C.2 investigate agreement between PRMScore and Best-of-N rankings, and compare their ability to distinguish models. Figure 1 revises the illustrative error analysis to include a false-positive judgment. Existing bias, step-position and ICL analyses remain; v1's Table 5 error case is retained as v3's Table 7.

E5.justification: v3 adds Somers' D correlations and standard deviations across model scores in Tables 6, 9 and 10. These introduce statistical association and dispersion summaries, without newly reported repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 3 changes Skywork-PRM-1.5B/7B overall scores from 31.7/36.2 to 61.1/65.1, without explaining the cause. It adds extensive model results and human performance of 83.8; Tables 6, 9 and 10 add Best-of-N outcomes. Some updated results conflict with retained entries: v3 Table 4 still gives Skywork-7B 36.2, and several appendix category tables retain its older scores.

T1.justification: The PRMScore and similarity equations, category formalizations and illustrative mathematical counterexamples are retained. Detailed definitions moved into Appendix A.1 do not introduce new mathematics. No substantive theoretical result, proof or derivation is added.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a fine-grained benchmark covering simplicity, soundness and sensitivity. v3 expands the stated evaluation scope to 25 models and adds an introduction claim that PRMBench exposes disagreement between step-level and outcome-level evaluation and can help reduce outcome-hacking risk.

C2.justification: v3 adds a substantive interpretation that successful outcome selection can conceal step-level errors and reward-hacking vulnerabilities, and argues that greater score dispersion demonstrates stronger discrimination. Difficulty is reframed against human performance rather than primarily random guessing. Section 7 newly discusses dataset scale and the absence of internal model analyses; most earlier bias and ICL interpretations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly identifies the Label-LLM annotation platform, annotator qualifications and human-evaluation assignments. Appendix C.2 documents candidate generation, aggregation and selection for the new experiment. Existing prompts, project access information and toolkit availability are retained; the added annotation information does not establish a changed data-construction procedure.

R1.justification: The basic positioning against correctness-only reasoning benchmarks remains. v3 adds connections to Best-of-N evaluation and reward hacking, including Zhang et al. (2025) and Gao et al. (2025), and references supporting new models and datasets. Some peripheral Lu and Su citations are removed, while Section 2 largely retains its earlier research framing.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work and category explanations are extensively rewritten and condensed. Detailed definitions move into Appendix A.1, the main error analysis moves into Appendix C.1, and the appendices are substantially reorganized. Terminology is standardized from evaluation subjects to categories.

P2.justification: Table 3 gains human and open-critic blocks, new Best-of-N tables and an annotation-platform figure are added, and Figure 1 is redrawn. Existing examples and prompts become Figures 7–24, detailed result tables largely receive standalone pages, and the error-case table moves to the appendix.

improvement.justification: The human reference, Best-of-N comparison and annotation documentation provide useful new context for benchmark difficulty and its relationship to outcome selection. However, unexplained score revisions introduce reporting conflicts: v3 gives Skywork-7B 65.1 overall and 62.8 on NCL in Table 3, versus 36.2 and 41.2 in Tables 4 and 13. These reliability problems limit the net quality improvement.
